title: Letter 2
paragraphs: How slowly time passes here, surrounded by frost and snow! Yet I've taken a second step toward my goal. I've hired a vessel and I'm now gathering my crew. The men I've already signed on seem dependable and certainly possess fearless courage.

But there's one thing I've never been able to find, and its absence now weighs on me as a terrible emptiness. I have no friend, Margaret. When I'm glowing with the thrill of success, there will be no one to share my joy. When disappointment strikes, no one will try to lift my spirits. I'll write my thoughts down, yes, but paper is a poor substitute for real human connection. I long for a companion who could understand me, whose eyes would meet mine with recognition. You may call me romantic, dear sister, but I feel the lack of a friend bitterly. I have no one near me who is both gentle and brave, whose mind is both cultivated and expansive, whose tastes match my own — someone who could approve or amend my plans. How such a friend would make up for the faults of your poor brother! I'm too eager in action and too impatient with obstacles. But it's an even greater problem that I'm self-educated. For my first fourteen years I ran wild on the common and read nothing but Uncle Thomas's voyage books. I discovered the great English poets only at that age, and only when it was too late to benefit fully from such studies did I realize I needed to learn other languages. Now I'm twenty-eight and in reality less educated than many fifteen-year-old schoolboys. It's true that I've thought more deeply and that my daydreams are grander, but they lack what painters call "keeping" — the proper balance and proportion among the parts of a picture. I desperately need a friend who has the sense not to dismiss me as a romantic and enough affection to help discipline my mind.

Well, these are useless complaints. I'll certainly find no friend on the open ocean or even here in Archangel, among merchants and seamen. Yet some feelings nobler than common human nature beat even in these rough hearts. My lieutenant, for instance, is a man of remarkable courage and drive. He's madly eager for glory — or rather, to put it in terms that suit him better, for advancement in his profession. He's an Englishman who, despite national and professional prejudices and a lack of refinement, retains some of humanity's noblest qualities. I first met him on a whale vessel. Finding him unemployed in this city, I easily recruited him for my expedition.

The ship's master is a man of excellent character, known among the crew for his gentleness and mild discipline. This quality, combined with his well-known integrity and fearless courage, made me eager to hire him. A youth spent in solitude, my best years passed under your gentle care — these have refined my character so deeply that I can't bear the usual brutality practiced aboard ships. I've never believed it was necessary. When I heard of a sailor equally noted for his kindness and for the respect and obedience his crew showed him, I felt incredibly fortunate to secure his services. I first heard of him rather romantically, from a woman who owes her happiness to him. Briefly, here is his story. Some years ago he loved a young Russian woman of modest fortune. Because he had saved a considerable sum in prize money, the girl's father agreed to the match. He saw his sweetheart once before the wedding, but she was bathed in tears. Throwing herself at his feet, she begged him to release her, confessing that she loved another man who was too poor for her father to approve. My generous friend reassured her. When he learned her lover's name, he immediately gave up his pursuit. He had already bought a farm where he planned to spend the rest of his life, but he gave it all to his rival, along with the rest of his prize money so they could buy livestock. Then he went to the young woman's father himself and asked him to consent to her marriage with her true love. But the old man firmly refused, feeling honor-bound to my friend. When my friend found the father immovable, he left the country and didn't return until he heard that his former sweetheart had married the man she loved. "What a noble fellow!" you'll exclaim. He is. But he's entirely uneducated. He's as silent as a Turk, and there's a kind of careless ignorance about him. It makes his conduct all the more astonishing, but it diminishes the interest and sympathy he would otherwise command.

But don't think that just because I complain a little, or because I can imagine a comfort I may never know, that I'm wavering in my resolve. My purpose is as fixed as fate. My voyage is delayed only until the weather allows me to set sail. The winter has been brutally severe, but spring looks promising. People consider it a remarkably early season, so perhaps I'll sail sooner than expected. I'll do nothing rash. You know me well enough to trust my caution and care whenever others' safety is in my hands.

I can't describe what I feel at the prospect of my expedition. It's impossible to convey the trembling sensation, half pleasure and half fear, that fills me as I prepare to depart. I'm going to unexplored regions, to "the land of mist and snow," but I won't kill any albatross — so don't worry about my safety, or fear I'll come back as worn and woeful as the "Ancient Mariner" — the sailor in Coleridge's poem who brings disaster on his ship by shooting an albatross. You'll smile at the reference, but I'll share a secret. I've often attributed my passion for the dangerous mysteries of the ocean to that poem by the most imaginative of modern poets. Something is at work in my soul that I don't understand. I'm practically industrious — diligent, hardworking, persistent — but alongside this there's a love of the marvelous, a belief in the marvelous, woven into all my plans. It drives me beyond the common paths of men, out to the wild sea and unvisited regions I'm about to explore.

But let me return to more personal matters. Will I see you again after crossing immense seas and returning by the southern cape of Africa or America? I dare not expect such success, yet I can't bear to imagine the alternative. Keep writing to me whenever you can. I may receive your letters when I need them most to keep my spirits up. I love you very tenderly. Remember me with affection, should you never hear from me again.
